analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal under federal fair housing law to reject renters because of where their money comes from, including housing vouchers, or because of veteran or military status.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would add source of income, veteran status, and military status to the Fair Housing Act, was introduced with 22 cosponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add 'source of income,' 'veteran status,' and 'military status' to the list of protected classes in the Fair Housing Act, the same law that already bans discrimination by race, sex, religion, and disability. Landlords could no longer refuse a tenant just because the rent would be paid with a Section 8 voucher, Social Security or disability benefits, child support, or other lawful non-wage income — a practice that is currently legal in most states. It also applies the same protections to veterans and service members. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters whose lawful income is not a paycheck: families and seniors using Section 8 housing vouchers or other housing assistance, people receiving Social Security, disability, or veterans' benefits, and households relying on child support, spousal support, or help from family. Veterans and active-duty service members also gain a new protected class. Landlords could no longer turn them away simply because of how the rent gets paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voucher holders, benefit recipients, and veterans

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'source of income,' 'veteran status,' and 'military status' as protected classes throughout the Fair Housing Act, so refusing to rent to someone because of these characteristics would be illegal discrimination.

Defines 'source of income' broadly to include Section 8 vouchers, Social Security and SSI benefits, child support and spousal support, payments from trusts or relatives, and savings — covering the sources landlords most commonly reject.
Extends the federal criminal statute against interfering with fair housing rights (42 U.S.C. 3631) to cover these new protected classes.
Gives state and local fair housing agencies a 40-month grace period to keep their federal certification while updating their laws to match, easing the transition.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property owners, who would face new fair-housing obligations: they could no longer refuse voucher holders or benefit recipients, and could face complaints, investigations, or lawsuits if they discriminate based on income source, veteran status, or military status.

drawbacks.text: Landlords and property owners would face new federal legal exposure: refusing or discouraging voucher holders would become a Fair Housing Act violation subject to HUD complaints, investigations, and lawsuits, a compliance cost smaller owners say falls hardest on them.

The bill relies on individual enforcement — a renter must bring a complaint or lawsuit against a landlord — so its real-world protection depends on how vigorously federal agencies and courts apply it, and some landlords have historically found indirect ways to screen out voucher holders within the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: renters with vouchers, disability benefits, or support payments would gain a federal right to be considered as tenants, and enforcement would fall on landlords rather than on tenants to prove discrimination. The main cost an honest supporter would acknowledge is that landlords bear new compliance and legal risk, and that some markets could see slower voucher uptake if landlords perceive the rules as burdensome. On balance the bill's costs are concentrated while its benefits are broadly shared among renters who least have market power.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote, which is where most bills quietly end.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the bill on September 17, 2025, joined by 13 original cosponsors and eventually 22 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee; the record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action since.

The bill would amend the Fair Housing Act to bar discrimination based on source of income, veteran status, and military status, and would extend federal criminal interference protections to those categories.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords who prefer not to rent to voucher holders keep the ability to screen them out, because no rule restricting that practice has advanced. Renters with vouchers remain exposed to rejection in most states.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords who screen out voucher holders

for.name: Rep. Scott H. Peters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 original cosponsors.

for.name: 22 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: Landlord and real estate industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal source-of-income protections as an undue burden on landlords, though no opposition activity by these groups appears in the bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support listed; the bill sits in a Judiciary Committee controlled by the House majority.

industries.note: They could no longer refuse applicants because their rent would come from a voucher, benefits, or child support, and could face HUD complaints or lawsuits for doing so. Some landlords had used income-source screening to avoid voucher tenants; that practice would become unlawful discrimination.

industries.industry: Housing voucher and rental assistance programs
industries.note: The bill does not change program funding, but by barring source-of-income discrimination it should make it easier for voucher holders to find landlords willing to accept them, increasing the programs' practical reach.

analysis.trajectory: With no hearing or markup after referral and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to advance in the House this Congress; similar source-of-income bills have repeatedly stalled in committee in prior sessions.
